opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when GPT-4 finished pretraining, a few of us started doing instruction-following fine-tunes on it pretty quickly, mostly reusing the data and recipes we'd built for the earlier models. Honestly, the assessment at first was pretty informal. We had internal eval sets, but a lot of it was just sitting down and talking to the model, throwing hard questions at it and seeing what came back.

What stood out right away was that the base model was clearly much smarter. You'd ask it something that needed several steps of reasoning, or something technical, and it would just get it, where the previous models would kind of muddle through. Even with a fairly rough fine-tune, the raw capability was obvious.

But it also had a lot of rough edges. These early fine-tunes weren't very polished. They'd sometimes hallucinate confidently, the formatting and tone were inconsistent, and the behavior around refusals or safety-relevant stuff wasn't dialed in yet. So you had this odd combination of "wow, this thing is really capable" and "this isn't ready to put in front of people." A lot of the work after that was closing that gap: better data, more RLHF, and more systematic evals so we weren't relying only on vibes.

I'd also say it was humbling, because our evals weren't really built for a model that strong. Benchmarks that had been informative for earlier models started saturating or stopped telling you much, so a lot of the signal came from people trying it on their own real tasks and noticing it was actually useful. That kind of qualitative impression ended up mattering a lot in those early days.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest response now.

So when we got the base model for GPT-4, the first thing we did was fine-tune it the same way we'd been fine-tuning GPT-3.5, with the instruction-following data and then RLHF on top of that. And honestly, the thing that struck me early on wasn't a benchmark number. It was just talking to it. We'd been staring at these models for a long time, so you develop a sense for where they fall apart, and GPT-4 just didn't fall apart in the same places. You'd ask it something that required holding several constraints in your head at once, and it would actually satisfy all of them instead of dropping one.

We did have more formal evals, of course. We'd look at human preference comparisons against the previous models, we'd look at factuality, we'd look at how often it refused things it shouldn't or complied with things it shouldn't. And on all of those the first fine-tunes were clearly better. But I'd say the evals understated it. A lot of what mattered was that the model could be corrected. With GPT-3.5, if it got something wrong and you pointed it out, it would often just apologize and produce a different wrong answer. GPT-4 would actually incorporate the feedback. That's a hard thing to capture in a static eval, but it's one of the main things that makes a model useful.

The other thing I remember is that the first fine-tunes were kind of undercooked. The base model was so much stronger that the RL data we had, which was collected with weaker models in mind, wasn't really pushing it. The model knew more than our data was asking it to show. So a lot of the work in the months after that was figuring out how to get the fine-tuning to actually tap into what the base model could do, rather than teaching it to imitate the somewhat more limited behavior of the models we'd collected data from before.

You can learn a lot that way, especially when the differences are large. But it’s also easy to fool yourself: you find one impressive response and start thinking the whole model is better. So you want to complement that with systematic comparisons, where people judge outputs from different models without knowing which is which.

sol-6.1.text:
At that stage, I was mostly just talking to the model and trying things. I had a set of prompts I liked to use, but a lot of the assessment was qualitative: could it understand what I was asking for, follow the constraints, and give a useful answer? And then, if it failed, was that a capability limitation or something we could fix with better training data?

One thing that made this tricky was that you could improve the model on the things you were explicitly training for while making it worse in less obvious ways. So I wanted to try fairly open-ended questions, too, and see whether it still felt like a smart, flexible model rather than one that had just learned a particular style of answering.
